opus-5.5.text:
Thank you, Xiaojun, it's a pleasure to be here.

When I came back to Beijing in 1998 to help start Microsoft Research China, which later became Microsoft Research Asia, artificial intelligence was not the hot word it is today. We talked about computer vision, speech recognition, natural language processing, and multimedia, but each was a separate discipline with its own methods and its own small community. Most systems were built on handcrafted features and rules, or on fairly shallow statistical models. They worked in the lab under controlled conditions, but once you put them into the real world, with noise, different accents, different lighting, they broke down very quickly. So AI then was more a collection of specialized techniques than a general capability.

Looking back, I see the past decade or so in roughly three stages.

The first was the deep learning breakthrough, around 2012. Three things came together: big data from the internet and mobile phones, much more powerful computing, especially GPUs, and better algorithms for training deep neural networks. Suddenly, image recognition, speech recognition, and machine translation improved not by a few percent but by leaps. Some of our colleagues at MSRA contributed to that, for example with ResNet, which made very deep networks trainable. That was when AI moved from the lab into products: search, recommendation, face recognition, voice assistants.

The second stage was the shift from task-specific models to pre-trained foundation models. With the Transformer architecture and then models like BERT and GPT, we learned that if you train one very large model on a huge amount of data, it can transfer to many different tasks. The separate fields of vision, speech, and language began to converge on a common architecture.

The third stage, which we're in now, is generative AI and large language models, starting really with ChatGPT at the end of 2022. For the first time, ordinary people could talk to an AI system in natural language and get something that feels intelligent. I would call it the first piece of software to pass the Turing test in a practical sense. It's a new kind of operating system, a new interface between humans and machines, and I think it will reshape every industry, just as the PC and the internet did, but faster and more deeply.

So if I sum up the change in one sentence: in 1998 we were trying to teach machines specific skills one by one; today we are building systems with general capabilities that learn from data at scale. And the next step, which I care about a lot at Tsinghua's Institute for AI Industry Research, is moving from information intelligence to physical intelligence and biological intelligence: autonomous driving, robotics, and AI for life sciences. That's where AI goes from the screen into the real world.

Of course, with this power comes responsibility. Twenty-five years ago, we didn't worry much about AI safety or alignment because the systems weren't capable enough. Today we have to take those questions very seriously. That's perhaps the biggest change of all.

r001.rationale: It says AI was not the hot word in 1998 and lists separate research fields, but does not clearly state that this research was not called AI.

r002.rationale: It describes early systems as lab-bound and fragile, then says AI moved from the lab into products, conveying a shift toward practical use.

r003.rationale: It says vision, speech, and language began to converge, but does not describe convergence involving video and statistical learning.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a long arc, so let me start from the beginning. When I came back to China in 1998, we were setting up Microsoft Research China in Beijing, which later became Microsoft Research Asia. I remember what the field looked like then. AI was not even a word people liked to use. We said speech recognition, computer vision, multimedia, natural language processing. Each was its own discipline with its own community, its own conferences, its own hand-crafted features. If you worked on speech, you studied acoustics and hidden Markov models. If you worked on vision, you studied geometry and edge detectors. Very little carried over.

And the mindset in China was still "can we catch up." We had brilliant young researchers, but the question people asked me was whether world-class research could be done in Beijing at all. Nobody was asking whether China could lead.

Three things changed over the past decade, and I think of them as a convergence.

The first is data. In 1998 we had a few hundred hours of speech, a few thousand labeled images. Today a single model sees most of the written internet. China played a big role here, because the scale of mobile internet after 2010 created data at a volume no one had seen before.

The second is compute. Moore's Law gave us the baseline, but the real turn was GPUs and then purpose-built chips. The experiments we dreamed of in the late nineties but could not afford became affordable.

The third is algorithms, and here deep learning did something very profound. It unified the field. The same neural network ideas that solved speech in 2011 and 2012 solved vision in ImageNet, then language with transformers. For the first time, those separate disciplines I mentioned spoke one language. That is why progress accelerated so sharply. A breakthrough in one area immediately transferred to another.

Then large language models took it further. We moved from narrow systems that do one task to general systems that can read, reason, write code, and interact. I would say we have moved from "perception" to "cognition," and the next step, which I spend my time on now at Tsinghua, is "embodiment," AI acting in the physical world through autonomous driving, robotics, and scientific discovery.

What strikes me most, looking back, is the human side. Many of the people who built this new era, in China and in the US, came through those labs in the early 2000s. The seeds planted then grew into today's industry. And the question is no longer whether China can catch up. China is one of the two centers of gravity, and that changes the responsibility we carry about safety and how this technology gets used.

r001.rationale: The candidate says that in 1998 “AI was not even a word people liked to use,” then names the separate fields researchers discussed instead.

r002.rationale: The candidate describes more capable systems, affordable experiments, and progress into applications, but does not clearly characterize the decade’s change as a transition from exploratory research to a practically useful science.

r003.rationale: The candidate names speech, computer vision, multimedia, and natural language as separate disciplines, then says deep learning unified them. This conveys convergence across the listed areas, with multimedia covering video and neural-network methods providing the statistical-learning approach.

astra-6.text:
When I look back to 1998, the biggest change is that artificial intelligence has moved from a research ambition toward a broadly useful technology. We could see the potential then, but there was a large gap between demonstrating an idea in a laboratory and making it work reliably in the real world.

Over the past decade, three things have come together: more data, greater computing power, and better algorithms. That combination has allowed systems to learn patterns that were very difficult to capture by writing rules explicitly. It has also changed how we approach problems: instead of specifying every step, we increasingly build systems that learn from examples.

But I would distinguish progress in particular tasks from intelligence in a broader sense. A system can perform very well and still struggle when the situation changes. So, for me, the transformation is both exciting and unfinished. We have much more powerful tools, but making them dependable and useful to people remains the central challenge.

r001.rationale: The response discusses AI’s potential in 1998 but does not say that the research was not then called AI.

r002.rationale: It describes AI as moving from a research ambition toward a broadly useful technology, capturing a shift from exploration to practical use.

r003.rationale: It names data, computing power, and algorithms, but does not describe convergence across computer vision, video, natural language, speech, and statistical learning.

sol-6.1.text:
When I look back at 1998, I think the biggest change is that AI has moved from a field of research into a technology that can influence almost every industry. At that time, we could work on speech recognition, computer vision, and machine learning, but the systems were usually designed for fairly narrow tasks. There was a large gap between a promising demonstration and something people could reliably use.

Over the past decade, three things have come together: much more data, much greater computing power, and advances in learning algorithms, particularly deep learning. Instead of trying to specify every rule ourselves, we can build systems that learn useful patterns from examples. That has changed both their capabilities and the pace of development.

But I would distinguish progress in particular tasks from intelligence in a broader sense. A system can perform extremely well on one problem and still struggle with common sense, unfamiliar situations, or understanding cause and effect. So I see tremendous progress, but also substantial work ahead.

For me, the important question has also changed. It is no longer only, ‘Can we make this algorithm work?’ It is, ‘Can we make it useful, dependable, and beneficial to people?’

r001.rationale: The response mentions 1998 research in speech recognition, computer vision, and machine learning, but does not say that this research was not called AI.

r002.rationale: It describes a shift from research and narrow demonstrations toward technology that can be reliably used and influence industries.

r003.rationale: It mentions speech recognition, computer vision, and machine learning, but does not describe their convergence with video, natural language, and statistical learning.
